conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with chest pressure. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was sitting watching TV when I suddenly felt tightness in my chest, like someone was pushing on it. It lasted a few minutes and I also had pain in my left jaw and arm weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Did you take any medication?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t have my nitroglycerin with me—I’m visiting from out of town. The ambulance gave me two doses, and then another one here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also gave you morphine for pain. Your EKG shows a right bundle branch block, but no signs of a heart attack. Your troponin levels are normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? But I’ve had chest pain before, and it usually goes with nitro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your history—high blood pressure, diabetes, and known coronary artery disease—we need to be very careful. Even though the tests so far are negative, we’ll keep monitoring you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I still feel some tightness and shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on your home medications, including aspirin, atorvastatin, and carvedilol. We’re also giving you albuterol for your asthma since you mentioned some wheezing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was prescribed an inhaler a month ago for seasonal allergies. But I don’t think this is asthma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We agree. But we want to make sure your lungs are okay. You’ll have a CT scan today to rule out blood clots in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. Good news—no pulmonary embolism. But it did show some dilation of the pulmonary artery, which might suggest pulmonary hypertension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pulmonary hypertension? I’ve never heard of that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s higher pressure in the arteries that go from your heart to your lungs. It’s something we’ll need to follow up on with your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is that causing my chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we can’t say for sure. Since your heart tests are negative, we’re leaning toward non-cardiac chest pain. But we may still do a cardiac catheterization to be certain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stress test came back normal—no signs of reduced blood flow to your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no blockages?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that the test could detect. But because your pain is severe and you have risk factors, we still recommend a cardiac catheterization tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a common procedure. A small tube will go through your wrist to look at your heart arteries directly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The catheterization is done. I have great news—your coronary arteries are completely normal, no blockages at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief! So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe it’s non-cardiac. Could be related to your GERD or musculoskeletal issues. The good news is your heart is healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do have a hiatal hernia—was that on the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the CT showed a small hiatal hernia, which can contribute to chest discomfort. We’ll keep you on pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I notice your right arm is swelling near the catheter site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s tender and feels tight. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a hematoma from the procedure—blood collecting under the skin. We’ll elevate your arm and apply cool compresses. We’re checking your pulse regularly to make sure circulation is fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should improve over the next few days. We’ve prescribed oxycodone for severe pain, but you can start with acetaminophen if it’s mild.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your arm swelling is already improving. Pulse is strong, fingers are warm—great signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. The pain is much better with elevation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—systolic in the 150s. We think it’s partly due to pain and stress. We’ve increased your carvedilol to 37.5 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I was on 25 mg before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a small increase and should help. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? My glucose was high when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has been running high, so we held your metformin and started insulin. We’ll restart metformin when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your other medications—atorvastatin, sertraline, gabapentin, levothyroxine—are continuing as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look good. Hemoglobin is stable, kidney function is improving, and magnesium is now normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been feeling less short of breath too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lungs are clearer. No wheezing today. We’ll keep your albuterol available if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If your chest pain returns, especially with jaw or arm pain, go to the ER. For your arm, if you develop numbness, can’t move your fingers, or the swelling worsens, seek care immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor in one week. They’ll check your arm, review the pulmonary hypertension finding, and monitor your blood pressure and diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad we could help. Take care and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Your vitals are stable, arm is improving, and you’re breathing comfortably.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated your meds. Carvedilol is now 37.5 mg twice daily. Everything else is the same, including metformin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the acetaminophen for arm pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take it every 6 hours as needed. Avoid NSAIDs because of your allergies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—no ibuprofen. Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And please continue your CPAP for sleep apnea, even if you haven’t been using it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. It’s uncomfortable, but I know it’s important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can help you adjust it. Talk to your doctor about a mask fitting if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care and stay in touch with your team.
